description: Curated swimming training principles for AI-assisted plan generation. Derived from publicly available USMS training guidelines, British Swimming coach education materials, and established sports science literature on swimming periodization.

zones.z1: Aerobic — comfortable, conversational effort. Develops aerobic base and technique.
zones.z2: Threshold — comfortably hard, sustained effort. Builds lactate threshold and race pace endurance.
zones.z3: High intensity — hard, unsustainable beyond short efforts. Develops speed and power.

recommended_drills.name: kickboard kick
recommended_drills.purpose: leg strength and horizontal body position

key_principles: Prioritise water confidence and basic technique over volume
Keep rest intervals generous (20–30s) so technique does not break down
Short reps (1–4 lengths) allow full technique focus on each rep
At least one kick-focused set per session to build leg strength
Increase volume before increasing intensity
beginner_endurance.coaching_summary: For a beginner swimmer aiming to build endurance, training sessions should comprise 20-36 lengths of a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 80% aerobic and 20% drills. The periodization approach will follow a 2 weeks progressive load, 1 week consolidation pattern. To ensure effective technique development, it's crucial to prioritize water confidence and basic technique over volume, and maintain generous rest intervals of 20-30 seconds to prevent technique breakdown. Additionally, incorporating short reps of 1-4 lengths will enable full technique focus on each rep, laying the foundation for increased volume before progressing to higher intensity.

periodization.pattern: Flat load — consistent volume each week, drills rotate

recommended_drills.name: catch-up drill
recommended_drills.purpose: stroke timing and front quadrant swimming

recommended_drills.name: fist drill
recommended_drills.purpose: forearm awareness in the catch phase

recommended_drills.name: 3-3-3 drill
recommended_drills.purpose: structured rotation and stroke count awareness

key_principles: Low volume — quality of each stroke matters more than distance covered
Long rest intervals allow full mental reset between drill reps
Alternate drill and swim reps to transfer technique immediately
Focus on one technique cue per session, not multiple at once
Count strokes per length to track efficiency improvement
beginner_technique.coaching_summary: For a beginner-focused technique development program, aim for a volume range of 16-28 lengths per session in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 60% aerobic and 40% drills. A flat load periodization approach is used, where the volume remains consistent each week, but drills are rotated to keep the training engaging and prevent plateaus. The key principle is to prioritize the quality of each stroke over distance covered, focusing on low volume and allowing for long rest intervals to enable a full mental reset between drill reps. Additionally, it's crucial to focus on one technique cue per session, such as improving stroke efficiency by counting strokes per length, to ensure effective technique transfer and progression.

periodization.pattern: 2 weeks base, 1 week introduce speed work, repeat

recommended_drills.name: sprint with full rest
recommended_drills.purpose: introduce fast turnover, 1 length at a time

key_principles: Build aerobic base first — speed without base leads to injury and poor form
Speed reps must be short (1–2 lengths) with full rest so quality is maintained
Never sprint more than 10% of total session volume at beginner level
Focus on stroke rate increase, not stroke length shortening
beginner_speed.coaching_summary: For a beginner swimmer aiming to improve speed, a suitable training plan involves sessions with 18-30 lengths in a 25m pool, balancing intensity at 65% aerobic, 10% threshold, 5% speed, and 20% drills. The periodization approach will follow a 2-week base building phase, followed by a 1-week introduction to speed work, repeating this cycle. A key principle is to prioritize building an aerobic base before introducing speed work to avoid injury and poor form. Additionally, speed reps should be short, lasting 1-2 lengths, with full rest in between to maintain quality, and should not exceed 10% of the total session volume.

periodization.pattern: 3-week build, 1-week taper. Final week: 60–70% of peak volume, maintain intensity
taper_principles: Reduce volume by 30–40% in final week
Maintain intensity — do not cut speed work
Include at least one race-pace set in taper week

key_principles: Include at least one race-pace set per week from week 2 onward
Practise turns and starts in every session — race time is won on the walls
Taper volume but not intensity in the final week
Underwater dolphin kicks off every wall are high-value for beginners — practise daily
beginner_race_prep.coaching_summary: For a beginner athlete preparing for a race, training sessions should consist of 20-34 lengths in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 70% aerobic, 15% threshold, 5% speed, and 10% drills. A periodization approach of 3-week build followed by 1-week taper, where the final week's volume is reduced to 60-70% of peak, while maintaining intensity, is recommended. The key principle of including at least one race-pace set per week from week 2 onward is crucial, as is practising turns and starts in every session, with a focus on underwater dolphin kicks off every wall to maximize efficiency. By following this structure, athletes can optimize their training and improve their overall race performance.

recommended_drills.name: pull buoy freestyle
recommended_drills.purpose: isolate upper body, build pull strength

recommended_drills.name: descending set
recommended_drills.purpose: negative split training and pace awareness

key_principles: Main sets should be continuous aerobic efforts — 200–400m equivalent blocks
Introduce threshold sets (Z2) from week 2 onward at 15–20% of volume
Pull buoy sets twice per week build pull power without adding leg fatigue
Negative split every main set — first half slower than second half
intermediate_endurance.coaching_summary: For an intermediate endurance swimmer, a suitable training plan involves 36-60 lengths per session, with an intensity balance of 70% aerobic, 20% threshold, and 10% drills. The plan follows a periodization approach of 3 weeks of progressive load, followed by 1 week of deload. A key principle is to structure main sets as continuous aerobic efforts of 200-400m equivalent blocks, with a focus on negative splitting, where the first half is slower than the second half. Additionally, incorporating pull buoy sets twice a week is crucial to build pull power without adding leg fatigue, laying the foundation for threshold sets introduced from week 2 onward.

periodization.pattern: 2 weeks aerobic base, 2 weeks speed development, 1 week recovery, repeat

key_principles: Speed sets require FULL rest — do not cut rest on sprint reps
Underwater dolphin kicks off every wall are critical for speed — minimum 3–5 kicks
Include one threshold set (Z2) and one speed set (Z3) per session in build weeks
Volume is secondary to quality — do fewer reps at proper speed rather than more at reduced pace
intermediate_speed.coaching_summary: For an intermediate swimmer aiming to improve speed, a typical training session should consist of 32-52 lengths in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 55% aerobic, 25% threshold, 10% speed, and 10% drills. The periodization approach will follow a 2-week aerobic base, 2-week speed development, and 1-week recovery cycle, repeated throughout the training period. To achieve speed gains, it's crucial to prioritize quality over volume, ensuring that speed sets are performed with full rest and incorporating key drills such as underwater dolphin kicks off every wall, aiming for a minimum of 3-5 kicks. Additionally, including one threshold set and one speed set per session in build weeks is essential, with a focus on proper technique and pace rather than completing a high number of reps at a reduced speed.

periodization.pattern: Focus on one technique element per week. Weeks rotate: catch → pull → rotation → kick → turns

recommended_drills.name: catch-up drill
recommended_drills.purpose: front quadrant swimming and stroke timing

key_principles: One focal technique point per session — not multiple cues simultaneously
Alternate drill rep and full-stroke rep to immediately transfer the skill
Track stroke count per length to measure efficiency gains over weeks
Cooldown should include slow, deliberate swimming with the session's technique focus
intermediate_technique.coaching_summary: For an intermediate swimmer focusing on technique, a suitable training plan involves 28-44 lengths per session in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 55% aerobic, 10% threshold, and 35% drills. The periodization approach rotates weekly, concentrating on one technique element at a time, such as catch, pull, rotation, kick, or turns. A key principle is to focus on one focal technique point per session, avoiding multiple cues simultaneously, and to alternate drill reps with full-stroke reps to facilitate immediate skill transfer. Additionally, tracking stroke count per length is crucial to measure efficiency gains over weeks, ensuring the swimmer is applying the technique correctly and making progress.

periodization.pattern: 3-week build, 1-week taper. Include race-pace sets from week 1.
taper_principles: Reduce volume by 35% in final week
Keep all intensity — cut reps, not pace
Include one full race-pace simulation set
Shorten warm-up in taper week sessions

recommended_drills.name: race-pace sets
recommended_drills.purpose: develop and cement target pace feel

recommended_drills.name: broken swims
recommended_drills.purpose: experience race pace with minimal rest

key_principles: Every session from week 1 should include at least 4 lengths at goal race pace
Underwater dolphin kicks after every turn — aim for 5–7 kicks minimum
Practise race-start dive or push-off in every session if pool permits
Mental race rehearsal: visualise the race during the last 100m of main set
intermediate_race_prep.coaching_summary: For an intermediate swimmer preparing for a race, a suitable training plan should consist of sessions with a volume of 34-56 lengths in a 25m pool, balancing intensity across aerobic (55%), threshold (30%), speed (10%), and drills (5%). The plan should follow a 3-week build and 1-week taper periodization approach, incorporating race-pace sets from the outset. A key principle is to include at least 4 lengths at goal race pace in every session from week 1, while also emphasizing the importance of underwater dolphin kicks after every turn, aiming for 5-7 kicks minimum. This will help build race-specific endurance and technique, setting the swimmer up for success in their target event.

periodization.pattern: 3 weeks progressive load, 1 week deload. Mesocycle: 4 weeks base, 4 weeks build.

key_principles: Main sets are long continuous blocks: 400–800m equivalent at Z1/Z2
CSS (critical swim speed) should anchor all threshold sets
Deload weeks must genuinely reduce volume — advanced swimmers often overtrain during recovery
Long cooldown is essential for recovery at this training load
advanced_endurance.coaching_summary: For advanced swimmers focusing on endurance, training sessions should consist of 56-88 lengths in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 65% aerobic, 25% threshold, 5% speed, and 5% drills. A periodization approach of 3 weeks of progressive load followed by 1 week of deload, repeated over a 4-week base and 4-week build mesocycle, will help achieve optimal endurance. It's crucial to anchor threshold sets with Critical Swim Speed (CSS) and prioritize long continuous blocks of 400-800m at low to moderate intensity. Additionally, a long cooldown is essential for recovery at this high training load, and deload weeks must genuinely reduce volume to avoid overtraining.

periodization.pattern: 2 weeks base, 2 weeks speed, 1 week recovery. Rotate mesocycles.

key_principles: Sprint sets must use full rest — never shorten rest to fit more reps
Underwater dolphin kicks: 7–10 kicks from every wall, maximum power
Speed sessions require 48h recovery — schedule carefully across the week
Max velocity work (Z3) should not exceed 15% of weekly volume
advanced_speed.coaching_summary: For advanced swimmers targeting speed, training sessions should comprise 48-76 lengths of a 25m pool, with a balanced intensity distribution of 50% aerobic, 25% threshold, 20% speed, and 5% drills. A periodized approach will be used, rotating between 2 weeks of base training, 2 weeks of speed-focused training, and 1 week of recovery. To optimize speed development, it is crucial to prioritize full rest during sprint sets, never shortening rest periods to accommodate additional reps. Additionally, speed sessions require careful scheduling to allow for 48 hours of recovery time, ensuring that athletes can perform at maximum intensity.

periodization.pattern: Each week targets one technical system: catch mechanics → body rotation → kick timing → breathing pattern → turns and walls

key_principles: At advanced level, small technique gains yield large time improvements
DPS (distance per stroke) is the key metric — track strokes per length every session
Pair drill with threshold swimming to test technique retention under effort
Turns and walls: every push-off is a technique opportunity — never coast
advanced_technique.coaching_summary: For advanced swimmers focusing on technique, each session should comprise 44-68 lengths in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 55% aerobic, 20% threshold, and 25% drills. The periodization approach will target one technical system per week, rotating through catch mechanics, body rotation, kick timing, breathing pattern, and turns and walls. A key principle is that small technique gains can yield significant time improvements, and tracking strokes per length every session is crucial, with a focus on distance per stroke (DPS) as the primary metric. By pairing drills with threshold swimming, technique retention under effort can be effectively tested, and it's essential to prioritize proper technique on every push-off, never coasting, to maximize efficiency and speed.

periodization.pattern: 4-week build, 1-week peak, 1-week taper. Race-pace sets mandatory from week 1.
taper_principles: Reduce volume by 40% in final week
All intensity sessions maintained — cut reps not pace
One full race simulation on day 4 of taper week
Sharpening sprint sets (3–4 x 1 length max effort) on day 2 of taper

recommended_drills.name: CSS descending sets
recommended_drills.purpose: building to and beyond race pace

recommended_drills.name: 15m underwater from push
recommended_drills.purpose: maximise underwater phase at race speed

key_principles: Underwater dolphin kicks: 7–10 powerful kicks from every wall — race margins live here
Every session includes race-pace exposure — no session is purely aerobic in race prep
Peak week: highest intensity, not highest volume
Taper without losing sharpness: reduce length of sets, keep the pace targets
advanced_race_prep.coaching_summary: For advanced swimmers preparing for a race, training sessions should consist of 52-80 lengths in a 25m pool, with an intensity balance of 45% aerobic, 35% threshold, 15% speed, and 5% drills. The 6-week periodization approach includes a 4-week build, 1-week peak, and 1-week taper, with race-pace sets incorporated from the outset. A key principle is to prioritize underwater dolphin kicks, aiming for 7-10 powerful kicks from every wall to maximize race margins. Additionally, every session must include race-pace exposure to maintain sharpness, and during peak week, intensity should be at its highest, rather than volume.
